explanation: The route crossed the lands of the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate, and the Yuan — but all were Mongol-ruled, and the khans guaranteed the safety of merchants and envoys. This Pax Mongolica is what made the journeys of Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, and countless unnamed merchants possible.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the route passed through several different khanates — no single Chinese dynasty controlled it end to end.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Europeans were travelers on the route, not its builders; no such European infrastructure existed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the map prominently shows the overland route — the sea route was an alternative, not the whole story.
option_explanations.D: Right: Mongol rule over most of Central Asia created the Pax Mongolica, a relatively safe political umbrella for overland trade.

options: (A) a single Chinese dynasty controlled every oasis town from Chang'an to the Mediterranean Sea
(B) European merchants built fortified rest stops every fifty miles
(C) the route was used only by sea, avoiding all land travel
(D) Mongol conquests placed most of the route under one political umbrella
stem: In the 1200s–1300s, travel along the overland route shown here was made safer than before mainly because:
stimulus: Map of the Silk Road's main overland route: it runs from Chang'an in China west through the Hexi Corridor and the oasis cities of Central Asia (Samarkand, Kashgar) to Persia and the Mediterranean, with branch routes and a sea route through the Indian Ocean also shown.

explanation: Islamic astronomers at observatories from Baghdad to Samarkand corrected and extended Greek astronomy, and instruments like this one — with Arabic inscriptions — embodied that knowledge. Astrolabes and the star tables behind them spread westward into Europe, where they later aided oceanic navigation.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the astrolabe was perfected in the Islamic world centuries before the Renaissance; the Arabic engraving proves its origin.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Muslim rulers actively patronized astronomy — observatories and court astronomers were common.
option_explanations.C: Right: the Arabic-inscribed instrument is evidence of Islamic advances in astronomy and of that knowledge spreading to other regions.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: astrolabes were precision working instruments for timekeeping, navigation, and prayer times.

options: (A) the astrolabe was first invented by scholars in Renaissance Italy during the 1500s
(B) Islamic rulers banned the careful study of the stars as un-Islamic
(C) Muslim scholars advanced astronomy, and their instruments spread to other regions
(D) such instruments were purely decorative objects that were never actually used
stem: This instrument best illustrates which development in the Islamic world?
stimulus: Photograph of a brass astrolabe made in the Islamic world, engraved with Arabic script. Its rotating plates allowed users to determine the positions of stars, tell time, and find the direction of Mecca.

explanation: The miniature comes from a French copy of Polo's book, painted by an artist who never left Europe: the 'Khan' wears a bishop-like mitre, the setting is a European hall, and the style is Gothic manuscript art. It tells us how Polo's account shaped Europe's imagined Asia — wealthy, courtly, worth reaching — not what the Yuan court actually looked like.

option_explanations.A: Right: the European clothing, setting, and Gothic style show a French artist imagining the scene — the image reveals European perceptions of Asia, not the event itself.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: no eyewitness drew this; it was painted in France by someone who never saw Kublai Khan.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: whether or not Polo traveled, this later illustration cannot prove it either way.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the style, clothing, and manuscript context are French, not Chinese.

options: (A) evidence of how Europeans imagined the Mongol court, not a literal record
(B) a contemporary eyewitness portrait of Kublai Khan, drawn from life at his court
(C) proof that Marco Polo never traveled to Asia
(D) a Chinese court painting of a diplomatic ceremony
stem: A historian should treat this image primarily as:
stimulus: A 15th-century French manuscript miniature from Marco Polo's Book of the Marvels of the World. It shows two European travelers kneeling and presenting a letter to a white-bearded Asian ruler seated on a throne — the artist's imagining of the Polo brothers meeting Kublai Khan. The figures wear medieval European-style clothing and the scene uses European artistic conventions.

explanation: By the 1200s the Christian Reconquista had reduced Muslim Iberia to the single emirate of Granada. The Nasrids survived by paying tribute to Castile while building the Alhambra — part palace, part fortress — as the seat and symbol of their fragile independence on its defensible hill.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the fortress-palace core is Nasrid work of the 1200s–1300s, not a post-1492 Christian addition.
option_explanations.B: Right: the fortified palace-city was the seat of the Nasrid emirate, the last Muslim state in Iberia, holding out as Christian kingdoms advanced.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Muslim Spain's greatest extent was centuries earlier; by this period only Granada remained.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the Alhambra is a palace-fortress complex, not a congregational mosque.

options: (A) Christian kings building the entire complex from scratch after conquering Granada in 1492
(B) the last Muslim state in Iberia, the Nasrid emirate, ruling from a fortified palace-city
(C) Muslim Spain at its greatest extent in the 700s
(D) the complex serving primarily as a mosque for the city's population
stem: The Alhambra best illustrates which development in Iberia during this period?
stimulus: Photograph of the Alcazaba, the fortress section of the Alhambra palace complex in Granada, Spain. Its massive reddish walls and square towers crown a defensible hilltop above the city; the complex was expanded in the 1200s–1300s by the Nasrid dynasty.

explanation: Krak des Chevaliers was the headquarters of the Hospitaller Knights, one of the military orders that held the Crusader states (Outremer) established after the First Crusade. Its concentric walls — a wall within a wall — were the cutting edge of medieval fortification, built to hold a small Frankish elite's territory against much larger Muslim armies.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Saladin fought the Crusaders but this castle was built by the Frankish Hospitallers — it was later captured by the Mamluks.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the castle stands in Syria and was built by Franks, not Mongols in Central Asia.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: it is a concentric military fortress, not a palace, and it was Crusader-built.
option_explanations.D: Right: the great concentric castle in Syria is physical evidence of the Crusader states — European Christian territories held by fortification in the Levant.

options: (A) Saladin's engineers building the castle as their headquarters for repelling the Crusader invasion
(B) a Mongol fortress guarding the desert caravan routes of the Central Asian Silk Road
(C) a luxurious Islamic palace complex built for the Mamluk sultans ruling from Cairo
(D) European Christians establishing fortified Crusader states in the eastern Mediterranean
stem: This castle best illustrates which development of the period 1200–1450?
stimulus: Photograph of Krak des Chevaliers in Syria: a massive concentric castle with inner and outer curtain walls and round towers, built on a hilltop by the Frankish Hospitaller knights in the 1100s–1200s.

explanation: Timur built his empire the Mongol way — through devastating campaigns from Delhi to Anatolia — and spent the proceeds the Islamic-imperial way, raising Samarkand into a showpiece capital. The Bibi Khanum's towering tiled portal, raised 1399–1404, was propaganda in glazed brick: the conqueror as patron of Islam.

option_explanations.A: Right: Timur's campaigns across Persia, Central Asia, and India generated the plunder and tribute that funded monuments like the Bibi Khanum in his capital.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Timur publicly patronized Islam — the mosque's Quranic calligraphy bands say so directly.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: Timur's wealth came from overland conquest, not Indian Ocean customs duties.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: this is Timurid architecture in Samarkand, a century before Ottoman classical style matured.

options: (A) a conquest state turning plunder and tribute from its campaigns into imperial monuments
(B) Timur's personal rejection of Islam in favor of older steppe shamanist traditions
(C) an empire funded mainly by customs duties levied on the Indian Ocean maritime spice trade
(D) Ottoman architects traveling east to impose their style on Central Asia
stem: The scale and decoration of this mosque best reflect which feature of Timur's empire?
stimulus: Photograph of the main portal of the Bibi Khanum Mosque in Samarkand, built 1399–1404 under Timur (Tamerlane). The towering pishtaq is covered in blue geometric tilework and bands of Arabic calligraphy.

explanation: The Korean court ordered the canon carved after the Mongols burned the first version — the blocks were both a devotional act and a plea for divine intervention against the invasion. Producing 81,258 precisely carved blocks also demonstrates Korea's mastery of woodblock printing, the most advanced book technology in the world at the time.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the Korean court commissioned the blocks against the Mongols, not at their order.
option_explanations.B: Right: the canon was carved as a spiritual defense — invoking the Buddha's protection while Mongol armies invaded — and shows Korea's advanced printing technology.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the blocks are carved with Chinese characters; Korea had a long literate tradition.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: the blocks contain the Buddhist scriptures, not currency designs.

options: (A) the Mongol khans ordering the blocks carved to print their own legal codes in Korea
(B) Koreans commissioning a vast Buddhist canon as spiritual defense against the invasion
(C) Korea had no writing system and needed the blocks to invent one
(D) the blocks being carved to print paper currency that the Korean court issued to pay its armies against the Mongols
stem: The carving of these blocks during the Mongol invasions best illustrates which Korean response to the crisis?
stimulus: Photograph of the depository halls at Haeinsa temple in Korea, whose shelves hold the Tripitaka Koreana: more than 81,000 wooden printing blocks carved with the complete Buddhist canon. They were carved between 1236 and 1251, while Mongol armies were invading Korea.

explanation: Around the late 1200s the Ancestral Puebloans moved into cliff alcoves — sheltered, defensible, near seeps and farmland. The round kivas visible in the photograph were ceremonial chambers entered by ladder, evidence of organized communal religious life in these aggregated villages.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Cliff Palace was built by the Ancestral Puebloans, centuries before and far from the Aztec Empire.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: this was a permanent farming village of hundreds of rooms, not a short-term camp.
option_explanations.C: Right: the alcove setting shows defensive and environmental adaptation, and the round kivas are ceremonial rooms — evidence of communal religious organization.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: kivas were ceremonial chambers, not granaries.

options: (A) an Aztec military outpost guarding the far northern frontier of the empire
(B) a temporary hunting camp occupied for only a few weeks during each year
(C) cliff-alcove villages with kivas showing organized communal religious life
(D) underground granaries cleverly designed to hide stored food from neighboring villages
stem: This settlement best illustrates which Ancestral Puebloan adaptation?
stimulus: Photograph of Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde, Colorado: a large Ancestral Puebloan village (c. 1200s) built inside a natural rock alcove. Multi-story stone buildings cluster around several round sunken structures (kivas — ceremonial rooms).

explanation: Monks Mound covers 14 acres and rose in stages over decades — work that required feeding and directing thousands of laborers, which only a hierarchical society with agricultural surpluses could do. Cahokia (c. 1050–1200) was the largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico, proof that complex societies developed in North America independently.

option_explanations.A: Right: a 30-meter engineered earthwork could only be raised by a complex, hierarchical society able to mobilize and feed massive labor forces.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: Monks Mound is an artificial platform mound built in stages, not a natural hill.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: the mound was complete centuries before any Europeans reached the region.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: it is a flat-topped platform mound that held buildings, not a sealed tomb like a pyramid.

options: (A) a complex Mississippian society able to mobilize massive labor for monuments
(B) the mound is simply a natural hill that was mistaken for a human construction
(C) European colonists piling up the mound with shovels in the 1700s
(D) it served as the tomb of a single powerful king, much like an Egyptian pyramid
stem: Monks Mound best supports which conclusion about North America before European contact?
stimulus: Photograph of Monks Mound at Cahokia, Illinois — a flat-topped earthen pyramid about 30 meters high, built by the Mississippian culture around 900–1200 CE. It is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico.

explanation: In seven years Ibn Battuta moved from Morocco to China, everywhere finding mosques, qadis applying familiar Islamic law, Arabic scholarship, and the duty of hospitality to travelers. Politically the lands were fragmented — Mamluks, Delhi Sultanate, Mongol khanates — but culturally Dar al-Islam was one connected world, and his route maps it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan Muslim traveling within the Islamic world, not a European crossing the Atlantic.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: his route crossed many separate states — Mamluks, Delhi Sultanate, khanates — not one caliph's empire.
option_explanations.C: Wrong: his journey down the Swahili coast to Kilwa is direct evidence of Africa's Indian Ocean connections.
option_explanations.D: Right: the route traces a culturally connected Muslim world — shared faith, Islamic law, and Arabic learning let one traveler cross from West Africa to India.

options: (A) a European explorer's daring solo voyage all the way across the Atlantic Ocean
(B) the complete political unity of the entire Islamic world under one single caliph in Baghdad
(C) the complete isolation of sub-Saharan Africa from Indian Ocean trade
(D) a connected Muslim world of shared faith and law in which one traveler could reach India
stem: Ibn Battuta's route, as mapped here, best illustrates which feature of the 1300s?
stimulus: Map of the travels of the Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta, 1325–1332 (red arrows). His route runs from Morocco across North Africa to Egypt, through Arabia and Persia, down the East African Swahili coast to Kilwa, and across the sea to India.

explanation: The map shows no emperor and no capital ruling the network — instead, dozens of self-governing cities (Lübeck, Hamburg, Danzig, Riga) cooperated through diets and shared privileges, with Kontore as far as London and Novgorod. The League monopolized Baltic–North Sea trade in timber, grain, furs, and fish through collective merchant power.

option_explanations.A: Wrong: the League was a confederation of cities, not a kingdom — no king ruled it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong: the map covers the North and Baltic Seas; the Mediterranean spice trade was handled by Italians.
option_explanations.C: Right: the color-coded member cities and distant Kontore show commerce organized by a league of self-governing merchant cities, not by an empire.
option_explanations.D: Wrong: this is a maritime network in northern Europe, unconnected to the Silk Road.

options: (A) a unified Hanseatic kingdom ruling the entire Baltic coastline as one state
(B) the League's tight control of the Mediterranean spice trade routes
(C) commerce run by a league of self-governing northern merchant cities
(D) a trading network centered on the overland Silk Road to China
stem: This map best illustrates which pattern of trade in late medieval Europe?
stimulus: A historical map of northern Europe around 1400 showing the Hanseatic League: dozens of member cities (color-coded by region) ring the North and Baltic Seas — Lübeck, Hamburg, Danzig, Riga — with outlying trading posts (Kontore) marked at London, Bergen, and Novgorod.
